# Design Levers {#sec-levers-ch}

A solar project is a very long list of decisions, and almost all of them fall into six groups. How much ground to take. Which ground. What gets built on it. What grows there and how the place is run. Who holds the asset. What the parties signed. These are the **design levers**, and they are the only things anyone can actually change.

Everything else in this document sits downstream of them. The [design pressures](design-pressures.qmd) are the forces arguing over how to set the levers. The [restorative functions](restorative-functions.qmd) are what the settings produce. And two of the levers have enough internal structure to need a chapter of their own, which is what the [scale transect](scale-transect.qmd) and the [sharing–sparing axis](sharing-sparing-axis.qmd) are.

| Lever | What it decides | What it can deliver |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Scale** | how much ground the project takes | the transect position, and how much of every other lever is left |
| **Siting** | which ground, and where on it | water quality, habitat context, service to nearby fields |
| **Structure** | what gets built, and how much earth is moved | microclimate, clearance for farming, light to the ground layer |
| **Management** | what grows, and how the place is run for thirty years | soil and carbon, habitat, most of the water balance |
| **Ownership** | who holds the asset and captures what it earns | a share of generation revenue for the people on the ground |
| **Contracts** | what the parties signed | the community function, and durability for all of the above |

: The six design levers. The first four act on ground and the last two act on paper. The full menu of decisions inside each one follows, and §-@sec-lever-matrix reads the whole set against the transect. {#tbl-levers}

## The full menu {#sec-lv-menu}

The specific decisions inside each lever, in one place, for a reader weighing an actual proposal. The sections that follow take them a few at a time; this is the whole set.

*Scale:* how much ground the project takes · the capacity it is filed at, and the [zone](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) that follows from it · interconnection posture, from behind-the-meter to transmission · whether to build once or to phase several arrays. Setting this lever rations every one below it, which is why it gets a chapter of its own (§-@sec-transect).

*Siting:* which ground the array takes · where on the parcel it sits · whether it stands upslope or downslope of the problem it might fix · how near it is to the fields it might serve · whether a landscape carries a few large arrays or many small ones.

*Structure:* mounting type (fixed, single-axis, dual-axis, vertical bifacial) · how high the panels sit · how far apart the rows are, and how much of the ground they cover · [pore-space](terminology.qmd#term-pore-space) configuration · [module technology](terminology.qmd#term-module-technology) (monofacial, bifacial, semitransparent, spectrally selective) · grading and site works · the built half of the edge (setback, berm, wall, fence line).

*Management:* what grows underneath, and how it is established · the mowing and grazing calendar · [stocking density](terminology.qmd#term-stocking-density) · how the array is operated ([tracking schedule, curtailment](terminology.qmd#term-tracking-curtailment)) · construction sequencing and traffic-lane discipline · the planted half of the edge (hedgerow, buffer, vegetative [screening](terminology.qmd#term-screening)).

*Ownership:* who holds the asset, and therefore who decides all of the above and captures what the array earns: owner-operator, landowner, developer, utility, cooperative, or shared · co-ownership or an equity stake in place of a rent.

*Contracts:* lease terms and duration · offtake structure · interconnection posture · [community-benefit](terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) instruments (host or community-benefit agreement, PILOT and good-neighbor payments, community-solar subscription, decommissioning bond) · easements.

## Scale sets the others {#sec-lv-scale}

**Scale** is how much ground the project takes, and it is the lever with the widest consequence, because every other lever is rationed by it. It is easy to mistake for a fact about a site rather than a decision, and treating it that way is how the most consequential choice in a project becomes invisible. Somebody decides to build five megawatts rather than eighty. That decision is made early, usually on grounds of interconnection and capital, and it settles how much [siting latitude](terminology.qmd#term-siting-latitude), structural freedom, and management capacity the design has left to work with.

Scale is a decision for some parties and a constraint for others, which is true of most of these levers. A farmer with one parcel and a distribution line at the road has very little say in it, and a developer assembling acreage near a substation has a great deal. The lexicon gives scale a chapter of its own because the attributes that move with it, interconnection posture, decision unit, ground-layer management, and [siting latitude](scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude), move together closely enough to be worth five named calibration points. That gradient is the [scale transect](scale-transect.qmd), and A0 through A5 are settings on this lever rather than a separate kind of thing.

## The three that act on ground {#sec-lv-ground}

**Siting** is the choice of ground, and it is the most powerful lever where a designer has it. It is also the first to disappear as scale grows. Placement decides whether a water-quality claim is even available, because the two routes want opposite ground: [avoided loading](terminology.qmd#term-fn-hydrologic) needs the impaired field itself, and interception needs ground between that field and the water [@schulte2017]. It decides whether a pollinator planting reaches anyone, since a forager works a radius of roughly 1.5 km and about 3,500 km² of US farmland sits inside that distance of existing and planned facilities [@walston2018]. And it is cheaper than the argument against it usually assumes: siting New York's entire 2050 build around biodiversity came to 0.17% above the least-cost case [@gallaher2026].

**Structure** is the hardware and its geometry: mounting type, how high the modules sit, how far apart the rows run and how much of the ground they cover, and what the modules themselves are made to do. It is the lever that carries the [microclimate function](terminology.qmd#term-fn-microclimate) outright, because shade, the drop in vapor-pressure deficit, and the shelter of nighttime minima are products of geometry rather than of anything growing. It also decides how much earth gets moved, which is the least visible structural decision and one of the most consequential. A mounting system that tolerates slope leaves the ground broadly as it found it, and one that needs a level plane means mass grading, so a racking choice made on cost sets the soil-carbon ledger for the next thirty years before any seed mix is chosen (§-@sec-fn-soil).

**Management** is what grows underneath and how the place is run across its life: seed mix, establishment method, the mowing and grazing calendar, stocking density, tracking schedule, curtailment. It carries soil and carbon, most of habitat, and most of the water balance, and it is the only lever that can still be changed after construction. That cuts both ways. Mowing timing is as decisive as the seed mix, because disturbance during nesting or bloom destroys the resource it was meant to supply [@blaydes2022], so a planting that was right in year one can be undone in year four by a contractor doing exactly what the maintenance schedule says.

Scale rations these three, and it rations them in opposite directions. At the farmstead, an owner has total control of the hardware and almost no choice of ground. Through the field and parcel zones, latitude opens and placement becomes the strongest instrument available. At utility scale, land assembly and grid access take the siting decision away again, and restorative practice becomes ground cover and grazing [@macknick2022; @boggis2020]. This is the [restoration mode shift](scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) (§-@sec-siting-latitude), and it is the single most useful thing the transect has to say about design.

## The two that act on paper {#sec-lv-paper}

**Ownership** is who holds the asset, and it settles both who has standing to decide the rest and who captures what the array earns. An owner-operator, a landowner leasing ground, a developer, a utility, a cooperative, and a set of community-solar subscribers do not want the same things, and the differences show up in the [ground layer](terminology.qmd#term-ground-layer) rather than only in the accounts. [Barnyard shelter solar](archetypes.qmd#arch-barnyard) is the clean case at the small end: it is restorative because the person who owns the array is the person who owns the animals under it, and no agreement was needed to align them.

Ownership is also the lever the transect moves furthest, and it moves in one direction. At the farmstead the array belongs to the operator. Through the field and parcel zones it belongs to the landowner, or to a community-solar structure with many small holders. At landscape and regional scale it belongs to developer capital and then to a utility or an independent power producer, and the person on the ground holds a lease instead. The [lever matrix](design-pressures.qmd#sec-lever-matrix) (§-@sec-lever-matrix) records that shift as a row, and it is the row with the most riding on it.

What moves along with ownership is the generation revenue, which is the largest thing an [agrisolar](terminology.qmd#term-agrisolar) project creates. A lease pays for the use of ground and is not a share of what the array sells, so a landowner earning three to four times what the crop returned per acre [@sturchio2025croplands] is still being paid for land rather than for electricity. **Restorativity has an ownership question inside it**, and the size of the lease payment does not answer it. That is what makes co-ownership, community-solar subscription, and an equity stake in place of a rent restorative instruments rather than goodwill: they are the means of keeping some part of the generation revenue with the people who host the thing. The [community and economic function](terminology.qmd#term-fn-community) is accordingly most at risk where a project is developer-owned and absentee, and most fully realized under local or shared ownership with early participation.

**Contracts** are what the parties actually signed: lease terms and duration, offtake structure, interconnection posture, the tax or PILOT arrangement, community-benefit instruments, easements, and the decommissioning bond. This lever carries the [community and economic function](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) almost by itself, and it carries something else that is easy to miss. It is what makes the others last. A seed mix is a management decision, but whether it survives to year twenty is a lease question, and nearly 40% of Central Valley agricultural land is rented, so a conversion that sustains an owner can end the operation of the person actually farming the ground [@stid2025].

Siting narrows to nothing by A5, structure narrows to commodity, management is weak at A1, and ownership moves away from the operator the whole way up. **Contracts are the one lever that holds its full range at every scale**, because a lease is a lease at eighty acres and at eight thousand, and every term in it is written by somebody. The clearest published case for the paper side runs through exactly that: federal biofuel policy has made conservation payments the less profitable option across much of the corn-ethanol acreage, and solar lease income can make a conservation practice affordable that was not affordable before [@sturchio2025croplands]. No ground was chosen and no hardware was changed. The restoration happened in a contract, which is the lever most often left on the table.

## What the levers produce {#sec-lv-outputs}

Three things come out of a lever setting, and the rest of this document is organized around them.

**A position on the transect.** Scale is read directly, which is why A0 through A5 are settings on one lever rather than an independent coordinate (§-@sec-transect).

**A position on the sharing–sparing axis.** This one is jointly produced, and the [two-question reading rule](sharing-sparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) in §-@sec-positions shows exactly how. Whether production continues inside the [footprint](terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence) is settled by structure and management, since clearance and row spacing decide whether a tractor fits and the ground layer decides whether anything salable grows, and that question separates S1 and S2 from everything below it. What the ground was beforehand is settled by siting, and that question separates ordinary converted ground (S3) from idle ground (S4) and impaired ground (S5). So the sharing wing of the axis is built and managed, the sparing wing is sited, and reading a position tells you which levers were doing the work.

**The restorative functions.** Each of the six in §-@sec-functions is produced by a particular lever or pair, which is what the middle column of @fig-functions-overview records: microclimate is structural, soil and carbon is structural at construction and managed afterward, habitat is managed, water is sited and then managed, and the community function is contractual. Ownership is the exception, because it produces no function of its own and instead decides who captures the ones that are produced.

## Which lever did the work {#sec-lv-mode}

Naming the levers makes a question askable that is otherwise vague: when a project turns out to be restorative, which lever did it? The answer is the project's **restoration mode**, and the levers name it almost directly.

- **Siting-led** — the restorative work is done by the choice of ground. [Solar prairie strips](archetypes.qmd#arch-prairie-strips) are the case, because the planting goes where the runoff already goes.
- **Structure-led** — the array's geometry does it: clearance, row spacing, how much light the modules let through. [Barnyard shelter](archetypes.qmd#arch-barnyard) is the case.
- **Management-led** — placement is a given, and the ground cover, the grazing regime, and the operational calendar carry everything. Regenerative solar grazing is the case.
- **Contract-led** — the work happens in the lease, the ordinance, or the benefit agreement rather than anywhere on the site. The [community and economic function](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) runs on this one.

**Two levers name no mode of their own, and the reasons are different.** Ownership does its restorative work through the fourth mode, because an ownership structure is constituted on paper: a co-operative or a community-solar subscription is a set of documents, so a project restructured to keep generation revenue local is contract-led even though ownership is what changed. Scale is the genuine exception. It names no mode because a mode answers how the restorative work was done on a given project, and choosing to build five megawatts rather than eighty is not a way of doing restorative work. It is what decides which ways remain available, which is the argument the [scale transect](scale-transect.qmd) makes at length, and it is why that chapter can say which mode dominates at each zone (§-@sec-restoration-modes).

That may not hold. Solar's spillover benefits scale with perimeter and proximity rather than with area, which makes several mid-sized arrays a different ecological proposition from one large one at the same capacity (§-@sec-community-scale). If that argument survives measurement, choosing to build small and many *is* restorative work, and scale earns a mode after all. Nobody has run the comparison (§-@sec-open-issues).

The mode is worth stating because it tells a reader what to copy. A design that worked because of where it sat will not transfer to a site without that ground, however carefully the rest is reproduced, and this is the mechanism behind [design import](terminology.qmd#term-design-import) (§-@sec-rg-consequences). It also tells a reader what to check. A siting-led claim is verified against a map, a structure-led claim against a drawing, a management-led claim against a maintenance schedule somebody has to keep for thirty years, and a contract-led claim against a document that can be read.

## Where the levers couple {#sec-lv-coupling}

The six are separable enough to name and not separable enough to decide one at a time. Row spacing and ground layer are a single decision rather than two, because crops differ in how much shade they will trade for relief [@weselek2019]. Edge treatment is simultaneously habitat design and [social-license](terminology.qmd#term-community-acceptance) design, and it costs land, shading, and room to farm. Grazing is a management decision that only works if the structure left clearance for the animals and the contract found somebody to keep them, which is why grazing arrangements fall apart for reasons that have nothing to do with grazing.

The couplings that matter most run from paper to ground, and the reason is that the levers get fixed at very different moments. Scale and siting are settled once and never revisited. Structure is fixed on the day the project is built. Ownership turns over in decades and contracts in years, while management is continuous and can be changed next season. Architecture has a name for this pattern: @brand1994 sorts a building into layers of differing longevity, after Frank Duffy's argument that a building is best understood as several layers of longevity rather than as one object, and holds that a design works when the fast layers can move without tearing the slow ones. @habraken2002 adds the part that matters most here, which is that each layer has a decision-maker of its own.

Read that way, management is the fast layer and therefore the fragile one. It survives only as long as somebody is paying for it and somebody else is checking, and the levers that do the paying and the checking are contracts and ownership. This is not a new observation about designed landscapes. The Landscape Architecture Foundation reports that parts of many projects fail within a year or two of installation because maintenance staff had no voice during design and the designer's scope ended at the final walkthrough [@douglas2015]. A project can be sited perfectly, built correctly, and planted well, and still be gravel in fifteen years, because the levers that would have held it there were treated as paperwork rather than as design.

## Does the set hold? {#sec-lv-completeness}

A set of six is only worth having if every decision a project makes lands in one of them. The test is to take the decisions this document names elsewhere, in the [full menu](#sec-lv-menu) above, in the [lever matrix](design-pressures.qmd#sec-lever-matrix) (§-@sec-lever-matrix), and in the design dependencies under each [restorative function](restorative-functions.qmd) (§-@sec-functions), and see where each one falls. Most land cleanly. Three cases did not, and they are where the set does work rather than just sorting.

[Screening](terminology.qmd#term-screening) lands in two levers at once, and that is the right answer rather than a defect. A berm, a wall, and a fence line are built and belong to structure; a hedgerow is planted, established, and kept, and belongs to management. Splitting them matters because the two halves fail differently. The berm is still there in year twenty whether or not anyone tended it, and the hedgerow is there only if somebody did. A project that promises visual mitigation and delivers it entirely in plantings has promised something with a maintenance bill attached, and the neighbor who objected is the person who finds out.

Two items in the older lever list turn out not to be levers at all. *Which ecological outcome is being aimed at* is an objective rather than a decision about the project, which makes it the [restorative goals](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) pressure. *Which regulations and certifications apply* is not chosen by anybody building, which makes it [policy and permission](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures). Both are real and both belong in §-@sec-pressures-ch, and a list that carries a goal and a constraint alongside actual choices is sorting three different kinds of thing under one heading.

Two definitions had to widen to hold everything. **Structure** covers grading and site works and not only hardware, because how much earth is moved decides both where the water goes and how much soil carbon is still there to build on, and no other lever owns it. **Management** covers the construction period and not only the operating life, because construction sequencing and traffic-lane discipline decide how much of the starting soil survives to be managed at all (§-@sec-fn-soil). Both widenings were forced by a decision that would otherwise have had nowhere to go, which is the useful kind of correction for a set like this to receive.

The set would be wrong in either of two ways. A decision that lands in none of the six would mean the list is short, and a decision that lands in all six would mean the categories are not cutting anything. Scale was the near miss on the first count. An earlier draft left it out on the grounds that it governs the other levers rather than sitting beside them, which was a bad argument, since ownership governs them too and nobody proposed removing that. Treating the size of a project as a fact about a site rather than as a decision somebody made is exactly the move this chapter exists to prevent. A counterexample of either kind is among the more useful things this chapter could be sent (§-@sec-open-issues).
